opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest problem is that the boundary itself is artificial. When you split people into "pretraining" and "post-training," you're basically drawing an org chart line through what is really one continuous process of shaping a model's capabilities. And once that line exists, people start optimizing for their own side of it.

For example, the pretraining team gets judged on things like loss curves or base-model benchmarks, and the post-training team gets judged on how the final model feels or scores after alignment and RL. But a lot of the most important questions sit right in between. What data mixture in pretraining actually makes RL work better later? Should certain reasoning or long-context abilities be built in pretraining, mid-training, or post-training? If nobody owns that middle zone, those questions don't get asked, or they get asked too late.

There's also a feedback-loop problem. Post-training people often discover what the base model is missing, like weak coding, poor instruction following in some domain, or a lack of certain knowledge. But if they're in a separate silo, that signal travels slowly back to pretraining, maybe one model generation later. Meanwhile the pretraining people may not have a good sense of what downstream actually needs, so they're guessing.

And for the researchers themselves, I think fixed roles narrow their intuition. The people who make the biggest breakthroughs are usually the ones who understand the whole pipeline end to end: data, architecture, training dynamics, RL, evaluation. If someone only ever works on one stage, they develop a very local view of the model. They might be excellent at it, but they can't see the trade-offs across stages.

So what I prefer is organizing around goals or capabilities rather than stages. You say, "This group is responsible for making the model really good at reasoning," or "at agentic tasks," and they're free to touch whatever part of the pipeline matters, whether that's pretraining data, mid-training, or RL. People still have their specialties, of course, but ownership follows the problem, not the phase. Especially now, as RL becomes a bigger share of compute and the line between pretraining and post-training keeps blurring, I think the rigid split becomes more and more of a bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response says fixed stage roles can narrow researchers’ overall view, but it does not connect post-training specialization to limited perspective on post-training data diversity.

r002.rationale: The response describes differences in team responsibilities and evaluation, but does not say AI teams hold stereotyped views about the kinds of researchers who do pretraining versus post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
When you split people into a "pretraining team" and a "post-training team," you're drawing a line that the model itself doesn't recognize. The model is one continuous object. What you put into pretraining data determines what post-training can even elicit, and what you learn in post-training tells you what was missing or wrong in pretraining. If those two groups sit on opposite sides of a wall, that feedback loop gets very slow, or it just breaks.

The first problem is incentives. If I'm only responsible for pretraining, my metric is loss or some benchmark suite, and I'll optimize for that even when it doesn't translate into a better model after alignment. If I'm only responsible for post-training, I'll treat the base model as given and spend my time patching things with RLHF or SFT that should have been fixed upstream, at the data level, for a tenth of the cost. Both sides are locally rational and globally wasteful.

The second problem is that the boundary itself keeps moving. A few years ago post-training was a thin layer, a bit of instruction tuning on top. Now with reasoning models and large-scale RL, a huge fraction of the compute and most of the capability gains are coming after pretraining. Things like data mixture, curriculum, synthetic data, these used to belong clearly to one side, and now they belong to both. So an org chart frozen around the 2023 understanding of the pipeline is already wrong.

The third problem is people. Fixed roles narrow what researchers learn. The strongest people I've worked with understand the whole stack, because the interesting problems are at the interfaces. If you tell someone early in their career "you are a post-training person," you're limiting their growth, and you're limiting what the team can see.

I'm not saying there should be no specialization. Running a pretraining job at scale is a real engineering discipline, and so is building a good RL environment. But I'd rather organize around the model and the problems, with people moving fluidly, than around stages of a pipeline that we don't even believe will stay fixed. Small teams, shared ownership of the final model, and everyone looking at the same evals. That's what has worked for us.

r001.rationale: The response says fixed roles narrow researchers’ learning and discusses data choices across pretraining and post-training, but it does not identify post-training specialization as limiting a researcher’s perspective on post-training data diversity.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes fixed role boundaries and labels such as “post-training person,” but it does not observe that many teams hold stereotyped views of the kinds of researchers who do each stage.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest problem is that you turn a division of work into a boundary around how people think. If someone is responsible only for pretraining, they may focus on improving the training loss without asking how those improvements translate into the final model’s capabilities. And if someone works only on post-training, they may treat the base model as something fixed, even when the problem they’re trying to solve would be better addressed earlier.

You still need people with deep expertise in each stage. But they should share responsibility for the final result and be able to move across those boundaries. When an experiment fails, the question should be, “Where can we most effectively solve this?” rather than, “Which team owns this?” Fixed roles can make that kind of exploration much harder.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training researchers may treat the base model as fixed, but does not connect exclusive specialization to limited perspective on post-training data diversity.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes fixed stage roles and team ownership, but does not say teams hold stereotyped views of the kinds of researchers suited to each stage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest problem is that people can start defining their work by the stage they’re assigned to, rather than by the problem we need to solve. If a model has a weakness, is it a data problem, a pretraining problem, or something we should address in post-training? You need to be able to investigate across those boundaries instead of assuming the answer from the organizational structure.

There’s value in specialization, of course. But if the roles become too fixed, you lose the feedback between the stages. The people doing pretraining need to understand what happens when the model is used and trained further, and the people doing post-training need to understand the capabilities and limitations of the base model. I’d rather have clear ownership with enough flexibility for researchers to follow a problem wherever it leads.
